questions.title: Internet vs WWW
questions.text: Explain the difference between the Internet and the World Wide Web.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Internet: global network of interconnected networks / the infrastructure (1)
- WWW: collection of web pages / resources linked by hyperlinks, accessed over the Internet with HTTP and a browser (1)
scheme.model_answer: The Internet is the worldwide network of networks; the World Wide Web is the collection of linked web pages that is accessed over the Internet using HTTP and a browser.

questions.title: Intranet features
questions.text: Give **two** features of an intranet that distinguish it from the Internet.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): private to one organisation; only authorised users / login; internal content controlled by the organisation; behind a firewall / more secure; smaller scope
scheme.model_answer: 1 It is private: only the organisation's members can log in. 2 Its information is internal and controlled by the organisation.

questions.title: Intranet technology
questions.text: An intranet uses the same technologies as the web, such as browsers, HTML pages and HTTP.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.

questions.title: History
questions.text: Who invented the World Wide Web?

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: Static and dynamic pages
questions.text: Explain the difference between a static and a dynamic web page, with an example of each.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Static: the same stored HTML file for every visitor, e.g. 'About us' (1)
- Dynamic: generated by a server script / from a database for each request, e.g. timetable, search results, online shop (1)
scheme.model_answer: A static page is a fixed HTML file shown the same to everyone, such as a school's history page; a dynamic page is built by a script for each request, such as a student's own timetable.

questions.title: URLs and IP addresses
questions.text: Explain how the WWW uses URLs while the Internet uses IP addresses.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Web resources are identified by URLs (protocol, domain, path) (1)
- DNS converts the domain in the URL into an IP address, which the Internet's routers use to deliver the packets (1)
scheme.model_answer: Users and links identify a page by its URL; DNS translates the domain part into the server's IP address, and the Internet uses that IP address to route the request and the reply.

questions.title: Two different things
questions.text: Many people use the words "Internet" and "web" as if they mean the same thing.

scheme.mark_scheme: Internet (up to 2): global network of networks; hardware infrastructure — routers, cables, satellites; uses TCP/IP; devices identified by IP addresses. WWW (up to 2): collection of web pages / resources; linked by hyperlinks; identified by URLs; uses HTTP / HTTPS and a browser; runs on the Internet
scheme.model_answer: Internet: a global network of interconnected networks made of routers and cables, using TCP/IP. WWW: a collection of web pages linked by hyperlinks, identified by URLs and accessed with HTTP in a browser.

parts.title: Services
parts.text: State **two** services that use the Internet but are not the WWW.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): e-mail; file transfer / FTP; VoIP / video calls; instant messaging; online games; remote login / SSH; DNS

parts.title: Page request
parts.text: Describe how a web page is delivered to a user's browser after a URL is entered.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): DNS converts domain to IP address; browser sends HTTP(S) request to the web server; request / response travel across the Internet via routers in packets; server sends HTML and other files; browser renders the page
scheme.model_answer: DNS finds the server's IP address, the browser sends an HTTP request across the Internet to the web server, and the server returns the HTML files, which the browser displays.

questions.title: School networks
questions.text: A school runs a staff portal that only teachers can use, and an e-journal that parents can log in to from home. It also has a public website.

parts.title: Identify
parts.text: Identify whether each is part of the Internet (public web), an intranet or an extranet.

scheme.mark_scheme: Intranet (1); extranet (1); Internet / WWW (1)
scheme.model_answer:
Staff portal: intranet
Parents' e-journal: extranet
Public website: Internet (WWW)

parts.title: Why intranet
parts.text: Explain **three** reasons why staff information is placed on an intranet rather than the public website.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): only authorised staff can see it / privacy; protected by firewall and logins / more secure; content controlled and reliable; internal / confidential data hidden from public; faster inside the LAN
scheme.model_answer: Only staff with logins can see it, so confidential information stays private; it is protected behind the school firewall; and the school controls the content so it is reliable and up to date.

parts.title: Technology
parts.text: Explain why the same browser can be used for the intranet and the public website.

scheme.mark_scheme: An intranet uses the same web technologies — HTML pages, HTTP(S), TCP/IP (1); the browser only needs the URL and access rights (1)
scheme.model_answer: The intranet is built with the same web technology — HTML pages sent with HTTP over TCP/IP — so the browser treats it like any website; it just needs a login.

questions.title: Web components
questions.text: A student opens an online encyclopedia page about Kazakhstan.

parts.title: Roles
parts.text: Describe the role of each in viewing the page.

scheme.mark_scheme: Browser: requests the page and renders HTML (1). Server: stores the page and sends it on request (1). HTTPS: protocol that transfers the page securely / encrypted (1)
scheme.model_answer: Browser: sends the request and displays the page. Web server: stores the encyclopedia pages and sends them. HTTPS: the protocol that transfers the page, encrypted.

parts.title: Hyperlinks
parts.text: Explain why hyperlinks are essential to the World Wide Web.

scheme.mark_scheme: Link pages / resources to each other, forming a web (1); users can move between related pages and sites easily without typing URLs (1)
scheme.model_answer: Hyperlinks connect pages and sites into a web, so users can jump to related information with one click instead of typing addresses.

parts.title: Dynamic
parts.text: The encyclopedia's search results page is dynamic. Explain what this means.

scheme.mark_scheme: Generated by a server-side script for each request (1); content taken from a database / depends on the search words, so it differs between users (1)
scheme.model_answer: The server builds the page when the search is made, using data from its database, so the results differ for each search.

summary: The Internet as a global network of networks and how it is organised, the World Wide Web as a service that runs on it (web pages, HTML, URLs, HTTP, browsers, web servers and hyperlinks), how a web page is delivered, other Internet services, and how the Internet, the WWW, intranets and extranets differ.

blocks.content: A **global network of interconnected computer networks** (a WAN of WANs). It is the physical **infrastructure** — cables, fibre-optic and undersea links, satellites, routers and servers — together with the **TCP/IP** protocols that move data between billions of devices.

items.title: How it is organised
items.content:
- No single organisation **owns** the Internet; it is a **mesh** of networks run by **ISPs**, companies, universities and governments.
- Large **backbone** networks (high-speed fibre) connect countries and continents; ISPs connect homes and schools to them.
- Every connected device has an **IP address**; **routers** forward packets between networks.

items.title: A short history
items.content:
- **1969** — ARPANET links four US universities.
- **1983** — ARPANET adopts **TCP/IP**: the start of the modern Internet.
- **1990s** — commercial ISPs bring the Internet to homes.
- Today — over **5 billion** users and tens of billions of connected devices (including the **Internet of Things**).

blocks.title: Services that use the Internet
rows: Game-specific protocols and streaming protocols over TCP / UDP

blocks.content: A **service that runs on the Internet**: a huge **information system** of **web pages and other resources** linked by **hyperlinks**, each identified by a **URL**, transferred using **HTTP / HTTPS** and viewed in a **web browser**. It was invented by **Tim Berners-Lee** at **CERN** in **1989–1991**.

blocks.title: Components of the web
rows: A document written in **HTML** (with CSS and JavaScript)
A collection of related web pages under one domain
A link from one page or resource to another — what makes it a "web"
The unique **address** of each page or resource
The **protocol** used to request and send pages
A computer that **stores** websites and **sends** pages when requested
**Client software** (Chrome, Safari, Firefox) that requests pages and **renders** HTML
A website that indexes pages so users can find them (Google, Yandex)

blocks.title: How a web page reaches you
items: The user types a **URL** or clicks a **hyperlink** in the **browser**.
**DNS** translates the domain name into the web server's **IP address**.
The browser sends an **HTTP(S) request** across the **Internet** (through routers) to the **web server**.
The server sends back the **HTML**, CSS, images and scripts in packets.
The browser **reassembles** the packets and **renders** the page; each image or file may need further requests.

blocks.caption: The web runs on top of the Internet

items.title: Static and dynamic pages
items.content:
- **Static** — the same HTML file is sent to everyone (e.g. a school's "About us" page).
- **Dynamic** — the page is **generated** by a server-side script for each request, often from a **database** (e.g. your timetable, search results, an online shop).

items.title: Web 1.0 → Web 2.0
items.content:
- Early web: mostly **read-only** pages.
- Web 2.0: users **create content** — social networks, wikis, blogs, video sharing, comments.

rows: **Selected outsiders** (parents, partners, suppliers) as well as members
Part of an intranet opened to outsiders
Shared information, e.g. marks for parents, orders for suppliers

blocks.title: The web is not only "the Internet"
blocks.content: E-mail, online games, video calls and file transfer all use the **Internet** but are **not** the **web**. A web page in an **intranet** is part of the organisation's private web, not the public World Wide Web.

blocks.title: Deep web and dark web
blocks.content: The **deep web** is the large part of the web that search engines do not index — online banking, school portals, private e-mail. The **dark web** is a small part reachable only with special software (e.g. Tor) and often used for illegal activity. They are different things.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Explain the difference between the Internet and the World Wide Web. [2]**
The **Internet** is a global **network of interconnected networks** — the infrastructure (1); the **WWW** is a collection of **web pages / resources** linked by hyperlinks that is **accessed over the Internet** using **HTTP** and a **browser** (1).

**Q: Give two features of an intranet that are different from the Internet. [2]**
An intranet is **private** to one organisation and needs a **login** (1); its content is **internal** and **controlled** by the organisation (1).

**Q: Name two Internet services that are not part of the WWW. [2]**
**E-mail** (1); **file transfer (FTP)** / video calls / online games (1).

- Using "Internet" and "web" as the **same** thing.
- Saying the web uses **IP addresses** to identify pages — pages are identified by **URLs** (DNS then finds the IP).
- Saying an intranet does **not** use web technology — it uses the **same** technology, privately.
- Giving only one side in a "difference" question.
